title: Special Edition: The Shield Hero’s Valentine’s Day Part 4
text: “Tempering is the most important step in making delicious homemade chocolate. You guys better remember this.”

Right now, I was melting some chocolate I’d gotten from the kitchen over a double boiler, showing the villagers how to make chocolate. You never know what might come in handy in life. Back when I was a “chocolate wizard,” I used to buy commercial-grade chocolate to make cheap chocolate that looked high-end. Anyway, chocolate is a pretty delicate food. If you’re off by even 1°C, it’ll affect the texture.
“If you mess up, a white substance called ‘bloom’ forms, and you end up with chocolate that doesn’t melt well and tastes bad. Be careful.”

For now, the village cooking team is leading the instruction. From now until Valentine’s Day, I plan to have them make chocolate whenever they have a spare moment. I kept the chocolates—supposedly made by Filo—simple. They’re simple heart shapes, decorated with colorful designs and stamped with Filo’s face—or rather, her mark. Well, it feels like the emphasis is more on the decorations.

“Those of you who can use fire or water Magic, pay attention to the temperature. First, use the water-bath method—that’s where you regulate the temperature by running water over the container holding the chocolate.”

With that, I quickly temper the chocolate, pour it into heart-shaped molds, and let it set. It’s nice to have Magic—it makes things so convenient around here. All I have to do is tell the folks around me to lower the temperature to the level I specified.

The quality of the chocolate I procured is pretty good, too. It might even be better than the store-bought chocolate in my world. No wonder—this is a world where finished products grow on trees… maybe the quality here is actually superior. Judging by the crepe trees, that seems to be the case.
I’ll go negotiate directly later to place a bulk order. I did get this through a connection, but I’ll be buying it officially this time.
With that in mind, I decorate the set chocolate. Eventually, I show the finished chocolates to the villagers.
“Just as expected of Shield Brother. You were so efficient—it was almost like Magic.”
“It’s not Magic or anything.”
Well, it’s not like I don’t have the Shield’s protection, though. Still, it’s a whole different story when it comes to adjusting the temperature and shaping the chocolate.
“Anyway, you guys, practice and learn this. I’ll teach you, and once you’ve got it down, teach the others. Work hard so we can mass-produce them.”

Now then… what should I do? Teaching is fine, but I’ll be bored until they ask me questions. Since the village’s desserts are going to be failed chocolates for a while anyway, under the guise of “snacks”… So, to kill some time—or rather, to challenge the advanced students—I’ll make and serve something a bit more difficult.
“Naofumi-sama… what are you doing?”
“Hm?”

Raphtalia had been participating in the practice, but she stopped what she was doing and looked over at me. I was processing beans that tasted like coffee into a powder and gathering butter and other ingredients. I also caramelized the nectar from the bio-plant to give it a caramel-like flavor, among other things. By the time Raphtalia called out to me, I’d gathered most of the ingredients and had reached the assembly stage.
“I was trying to make a sort-of Opera cake.”
“Opera… In Naofumi-sama’s world, isn’t that… the name of a play?”
“No. It’s a dessert with that name.”
“A dessert from Lord Naofumi’s world?”
“Well, yeah. It might exist in this world, too.”

Since there didn’t seem to be any crepes, it might not exist here. But maybe a pastry chef in this world has invented it. There are reincarnated people here, after all. It’s not impossible that someone got really into baking. I’ve read those kinds of girls’ novels, and when you think about it, it’s hard to imagine that heroes and reincarnated people are all men.
“Wow, that’s awesome!”

For the finishing touch, I used the “tablière” method—spreading the chocolate on a table to regulate the temperature—to create a musical-score-like design, which I then pinned onto the opera to complete it. The village slaves got super excited when they saw my makeshift opera and started making a big fuss. The cooking crew is taking notes on how to make it. Is it really that hard?
“Aren’t you going to eat it?”
“Later. I plan to eat it as a palate cleanser after everyone’s finished tasting.”
“Can’t wait!”
With that, everyone happily went back to their work.
“Hey, Naofumi.”
“What’s up?”
Melty came over to me with a troubled look on her face.
“Apparently, there’s also a way to make chocolate from beans…”

She said, showing me a bag containing what looked like cacao beans. If they’re even making their own cacao beans, just how seriously is the guy who grew a chocolate tree taking this Valentine’s Day challenge? I’d thought this was just some wild idea from a hero who couldn’t get a date even in another world, but now it feels a little different.
“Sigh… Alright. We can’t just waste the ingredients, after all. I’ll show you how to make chocolate from cacao beans, too.”
This is actually quite a hassle, though. All I know is what I’ve read online…

“First, you roast the cacao beans. You know, until they look like those coffee-like beans. It’s pretty tedious and takes a while, so hang tight. Oh, and the flavor changes during roasting, so be careful.”

Looks like we’ll be spending the whole day just making chocolate today. I take out the roasted cacao beans and crush the cacao nibs—the part that actually becomes chocolate—to extract them. Phew. I don’t know who created cacao, but it seems to have almost the same structure as my world. If it were different, I definitely wouldn’t be able to make it.
“So, we’re going to crush this. For this part, just use wind or earth magic to seal it in an airtight container and keep crushing it until I say it’s good.”
The slaves fine-tune their Magic exactly as I instructed.
“Melty, use your Magic to remove any moisture—moisture is a no-go when it comes to chocolate.”
“Naofumi, you seem pretty experienced with this.”
“It’s not exactly like that. This is actually my first time making it from cacao beans.”
“You really don’t look like it, though…”

Melty’s giving me a kind of skeptical look. You’d learn this much just by reading about it online. Well, I guess Melty doesn’t know about the internet. Or rather, surely there must be a recipe for making it from cacao beans in this world too. That is, if someone actually invented something called ‘cacao beans’ in the first place.

“Next, grind it even finer using a mortar and pestle or something… If you can still do it with Magic, go ahead and do more. Then, divide the mixture into three parts, squeeze it to separate the fat, the residue, and the chocolate. And there you have it: cocoa butter and cocoa powder. You can even make a simple chocolate cake with the cocoa powder. Oh, and be careful with the temperature when handling the cocoa butter. It’s actually harder to temper than the cocoa powder.”

I’ll handle the tricky parts and put together a temperature chart. My memory’s a bit fuzzy, so I’ll need to do a little research. It’d be great if there were a recipe on the shield… but is there one? Let’s have the shield absorb the finished ingredients and check later.

“Next, add sugar to the finished ingredients… mix in the right amount of dried honey and powdered milk, then adjust the temperature… To be honest, this is starting to get a pain. Why don’t you guys just handle the rest on your own?”
“Naofumi, don’t give up halfway through.”
“Yeah, yeah.”
From here on out, it’s basically a competition to see how smooth you can make it. If I keep fiddling with it forever, the taste will suffer, so let’s call it a day while it’s still decent.
“Oh, it’s starting to look more and more like chocolate.”
“It’s already chocolate. From here on out, it’s no different from working with regular chocolate. There you go—it’s done.”
So, after adjusting the temperature, I poured it into a mold and let it cool.
“It looks like this.”
“Hmm… Considering mass production, making it from cocoa beans isn’t really an option.”

She analyzed the process Melty was using and nodded repeatedly. Well, that makes sense. Even I feel like I’ve wasted a lot of time. Just as I was thinking that, I noticed that Ren, the Sword Hero, was mingling with the villagers. When did he slip in there?
“Naofumi, I knew you were a good cook, but you can do this too? Starting from cocoa beans… come on, just how good are you at cooking?”
“Good? You can do this much just by looking it up online, right?”
“That’s a lie!”
Ren glared at me with a look that made it seem like he was about to swing a machete. Isn’t that joke a little outdated? Not that I know how things work in Ren’s world, though.
“It’s not a lie. Sure, making it from cocoa beans is a hassle—it’s my first time—but it’s doable, right?”
“No, it’s not!”
What’s with the dramatic tone? Anyway, you should help out too. If your weapon skills let you work with chocolate, that is.
“So? Why are we making chocolate…? It must be Valentine’s Day.”
“Yeah, we’re going to be preparing for Valentine’s Day for a while now. Ren, what about you?”
“Me? I…”
Before Ren could say anything, I voiced my thoughts first.
“Most likely, hunting monsters that’ve been activated by the Valentine’s Day event, right?”
Ren nodded at my question… Just as I thought. This world takes seasonal events way too seriously. I mean, what’s with monsters that only appear around February 14th? It’s all kind of weird, isn’t it?
“So? What do you think about chocolate and stuff?”

In response to my question, Ren’s gaze kept darting toward Taniko and the female knight, who were taking a break in the monster pen. Well, that’s a reasonable reaction. The question is whether those two are even interested in Valentine’s Day… Frankly, I doubt it.

Alright, I’d better come up with a plan. You never know what Ren might do if he doesn’t get any. Judging by what happened at Christmas—if I hadn’t done anything back then, who knows what would’ve happened. I’d like to think it’s out of the question, but the Curse Series might kick in. Ren has gotten stronger in many ways, but in certain emotional areas, he’s become as fragile as tofu.
“Cure!”

For some reason, little Gaelion is staring intently at the chocolate I’m cooking. Since he seemed unusually motivated this time, I let him handle the temperature control—or rather, the heat—for me. He adjusted the heat just as I ordered, so he was actually helpful.
“Do you want some?”
“Cure!”

Gaelion nods vigorously. Are dragons… sweet tooths? I seem to recall hearing something like that before… Oh well, whatever. I’ll let him have a bite of the chocolate I made from cocoa beans as a thank-you for controlling the temperature.
“Cureeee…”
Oh, Gaelion has his hand pressed against his cheek and is happily stuffing his face. I’ll give it a try, too. Well, I did taste it halfway through, but…
Hmm, honestly, it’s a bit iffy. It’s slightly gritty. It really tastes homemade. If this were a store, it’d fail. Just like Melty said, it’s not worth the effort.

When I had my shield absorb it, a recipe for turning cacao beans into chocolate appeared. The quality will be pretty consistent, but that’s fine, right? It’s just a hassle to go through all that trouble. If we get all the existing heroes to work on creating recipes, we should be able to secure enough of it. It looks like we’ll be able to prepare a decent amount of chocolate, too.

Oh, Gaelion must have figured out how to do it—he’s started making chocolate on his own. What on earth is the parent Gaelion thinking, letting the young Gaelion cook? The Dragon Emperor would probably say that dragons shouldn’t be cooking or anything like that.
“Lord Naofumi, it’s ready.”

Raphtalia shows me the chocolate she made on her first try. It’s a bit pale. A failure. But the others’ are pretty much the same. It looks like we’ve got a long road ahead of us making handmade chocolates for sale.
“Oh, and you guys—”
“What?”
“It’s fine to give chocolates to someone you like—as long as it’s not for sale—but don’t mix your own hair, blood, or bodily fluids into them.”

This is the most important rule. The thing that makes men feel the most disgusted when eating Valentine’s Day chocolates is, without a doubt, finding foreign objects inside them. Girls’ love spells are terrifying. Every year, when I see the chocolates made by the girls who’ve come to ask me how to make them, I always think the same thing.
“I wouldn’t do something that gross, bro!”

Keel, who had been watching from the sidelines, blurted out. Oh, come to think of it, Imiya—the head slave who’s really good with her hands—and the Rumo species have a fatal flaw. Their hair gets mixed into the chocolate. I really needed to be careful about that.
“Also, this is just a prototype, but when you sell the finished product, make sure to put what’s in this bottle inside.”
I hand the slaves a thin, golden… thread-like thing (I won’t go into specifics) and some white and cherry-pink fibrous material (again, I won’t go into specifics).
“Here’s the one for Keel.”
I pull out a bottle containing black and white fibrous material (still can’t go into specifics).
“What’s this?”
“It’s magic powder. Mixing it in gives the handmade chocolate even greater value. Keel and Filo, you absolutely must not touch it. It’ll weaken the effect.”
I didn’t say it would make it taste better. I’ll leave the contents to your imagination. As for the details… that’ll come back to bite me. It’s something I can’t tell Philo and Keel about.
“Don’t even sniff it, either.”
“O-okay.”
The slaves all nodded in unison and took the bottle.
“Well, that’s about it. It’s almost snack time. Go call the folks from the village.”
Having finished their cooking lesson, the slaves went to call the people in the village.
